q-95079.name: Question 1
q-95079.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4+(-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 1 \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=xcos⁡y,x=4t and y=t, compute dfdt.

a
sin⁡t+4tcos⁡t
b
4(sin⁡t−tcos⁡t)
c
4(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t)
d
4(cos⁡t+tsin⁡t)
e
sin⁡t−4tcos⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=cos⁡y,∂f∂y=−xsin⁡y

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=cos⁡t∂f∂y=−4tsin⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=4,dydt=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=cos⁡t⋅4+(−4tsin⁡t)⋅1=4(cos⁡t−tsin⁡t).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=sin⁡xcos⁡y,x=t2, and y=t, compute dfdt.

a
2tcos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)−sin⁡(t2)sin⁡(t)
b
t2cos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)−tsin⁡(t2)
c
−2tsin⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)
d
cos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)−sin⁡(t2)sin⁡(t)
e
−2tcos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=cos⁡xcos⁡y,∂f∂y=−sin⁡xsin⁡y

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=cos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(t2)sin⁡(t).

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2t,dydt=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=cos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)⋅2t+(−sin⁡(t2)sin⁡(t))⋅1=2tcos⁡(t2)cos⁡(t)−sin⁡(t2)sin⁡(t).

q-170669.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-{e}^{2y-x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{2y-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =-{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y)=e2y−x,x=cos⁡t and y=sin⁡t, compute dfdt.

e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t
b

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=−e2y−x,∂f∂y=2e2y−x

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=−e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t,∂f∂y=2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=−sin⁡t,dydt=cos⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=−e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+2e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=(sin⁡t+2cos⁡t)e2sin⁡t−cos⁡t.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{t}^{2}\cdot t}+{t}^{2}\cdot t{e}^{{t}^{2}\cdot t}={e}^{{t}^{3}}+{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{3}}=(1+{t}^{3}){e}^{{t}^{3}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =({t}^{2})^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}\cdot t}={t}^{4}{e}^{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =(1+{t}^{3}){e}^{{t}^{3}}\cdot 2t+{t}^{4}{e}^{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1 \\  & =(2t+2{t}^{4}){e}^{{t}^{3}}+{t}^{4}{e}^{{t}^{3}} \\  & =(2t+3{t}^{4}){e}^{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

dxdt=2t,dydt=1.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{1+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{(1+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{1+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+s}\cdot 2s-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2s}{1+s}-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2s(1+s)-{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{s(2+s)}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

If f(x,y)=x1+y, x=s2 and y=s, compute dfds.

a
2+s21+s
b
s(2+s)(1+s)2
c
 s(1−s)(1+s)2
d
s2(2+s)(1+s)
e
1+s2(1+s)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=11+y,∂f∂y=−x(1+y)2

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get ∂f∂x=11+s,∂f∂y=−s2(1+s)2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get dxds=2s,dyds=1.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=11+s⋅2s−s2(1+s)2⋅1=2s1+s−s2(1+s)2=2s(1+s)−s2(1+s)2=s(2+s)(1+s)2.

q-95117.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+x{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(1+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

If f(x,y)=xey and y=sin⁡x, compute dfdx.

a
esin⁡x(1+xcos⁡x)
b
esin⁡x(1−cos⁡x)
c
ecos⁡x(1+sin⁡x)
d
esin⁡x(1+xsin⁡x)
e
ecos⁡x(1−xsin⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ey,∂f∂y=xey

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=esin⁡x,∂f∂y=xesin⁡x.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=cos⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=esin⁡x+xesin⁡x⋅cos⁡x=esin⁡x(1+xcos⁡x).

q-95123.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy-4}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy-4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{x\cdot {x}^{2}-4}}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{x\cdot {x}^{2}-4}}=\frac{x}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}+\frac{x}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=1x+y,∂f∂y=1x+y

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=∂f∂y=1x+e2x.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=2e2x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=1x+e2x+1x+e2x⋅2e2x=1x+e2x+2e2xx+e2x=1+2e2xx+e2x.

q-170671.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=(1-{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

−3sin⁡xcos2⁡x

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows:

dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=(1−y2)cos⁡x,∂f∂y=−2ysin⁡x

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get

∂f∂x=(1−cos2⁡x)cos⁡x=sin2⁡xcos⁡x,∂f∂y=−2cos⁡xsin⁡x

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get

dydx=−sin⁡x.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdx=sin2⁡xcos⁡x+(−2cos⁡xsin⁡x)⋅(−sin⁡x)=sin2⁡xcos⁡x+2sin2⁡xcos⁡x=3sin2⁡xcos⁡x.

q-94752.name: Question 11
q-94752.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =({e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t})(s\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+({e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t})(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(s\operatorname{cos}⁡t-s\operatorname{sin}⁡t){e}^{s\operatorname{sin}⁡t+s\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =s(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t){e}^{s(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

Let f(x,y)=ex+y, where x=ssin⁡t and y=scos⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
s(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
b
(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
c
(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
d
s(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
e
s2(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=ex+y,∂f∂y=ex+y

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=essin⁡t+scos⁡t,∂f∂y=essin⁡t+scos⁡t.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=scos⁡t,∂y∂t=−ssin⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t=(essin⁡t+scos⁡t)(scos⁡t)+(essin⁡t+scos⁡t)(−ssin⁡t)=(scos⁡t−ssin⁡t)essin⁡t+scos⁡t=s(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)es(sin⁡t+cos⁡t).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =1, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(-1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Let f(x,y)=x−y, where x=−scos⁡t and y=ssin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
2cos⁡t
b
−(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)
c
s(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)
d
s(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
e
cos⁡t−sin⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=1,∂f∂y=−1

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=1,∂f∂y=−1.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=−cos⁡t,∂y∂s=sin⁡t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(1)(−cos⁡t)+(−1)(sin⁡t)=−(cos⁡t+sin⁡t).

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(ts)(s-t)=2t{s}^{2}-2s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(ts)^{2}={t}^{2}{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(2t{s}^{2}-2s{t}^{2})(s)+({t}^{2}{s}^{2})(-1) \\  & =2t{s}^{3}-2{s}^{2}{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}{s}^{2} \\  & =2t{s}^{3}-3{t}^{2}{s}^{2} \\  & =t{s}^{2}(2s-3t).\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2(t{e}^{s})}{(t{e}^{s})^{2}+(t{e}^{-s})^{2}}=\frac{2{e}^{s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2(t{e}^{-s})}{(t{e}^{s})^{2}+(t{e}^{-s})^{2}}=\frac{2{e}^{-s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{-s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}\cdot {e}^{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}\cdot {e}^{-s} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{2s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}+\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})} \\  & =\frac{2({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4y\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 15
?

Let f(x,y)=x2−2y2, where x=ssin⁡t and y=tsin⁡s. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
2s2sin2⁡t+2tsin⁡2s
b
ssin⁡2t−4t2sin2⁡s
c
2scos2⁡t−2tsin⁡2s
d
2ssin2⁡t−2t2sin⁡2s
e
s2sin⁡2t+4tsin2⁡s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t) and y=y(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=2x,∂f∂y=−4y

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=2ssin⁡t,∂f∂y=−4tsin⁡s.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=sin⁡t,∂y∂s=tcos⁡s.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s=(2ssin⁡t)(sin⁡t)+(−4tsin⁡s)(tcos⁡s)=2ssin2⁡t−4t2sin⁡scos⁡s=2ssin2⁡t−2t2sin⁡2s.

q-94811.name: Question 16
q-94811.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(3)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-2t)+(1)\cdot 0 \\  & =4t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Let f(x,y,z)=3x−2y+z, where x=s+t, y=s2−t2 and z=s. Calculate ∂f∂t.

a
8t−s
b
2s−1
c
2t−s−3
d
4t+3
e
5t+4s−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=3,∂f∂y=−2,∂f∂z=1.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=1,∂y∂t=−2t,∂z∂t=0.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(3)⋅1+(−2)⋅(−2t)+(1)⋅0=4t+3.

q-37208.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{2}z,$ where $x=3t,$ $y=t-s$ and $z=2st.$ Given that

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+{c}_{1}s{t}^{2}+{c}_{2}{s}^{2}t+{c}_{3}{s}^{3},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$
q-37208.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(t-s)(2st)=4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =(t-s)^{2}={t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =3, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)\cdot 3+(4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t)\cdot 1+({t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2})\cdot 2s \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3} \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+6s{t}^{2}-8{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=6,$ ${c}_{2}=-8$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=6+(-8)+2=0.
$$

Question 17
?

Let f(x,y,z)=cos⁡x+y2z, where x=3t, y=t−s and z=2st. Given that ∂f∂t=−3sin⁡3t+c1st2+c2s2t+c3s3, find the value of c1+c2+c3.

a
3
b
−2
c
0
d
−5
e
4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=−sin⁡x,∂f∂y=2yz,∂f∂z=y2.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get

∂f∂x=−sin⁡3t,∂f∂y=2(t−s)(2st)=4st2−4s2t,∂f∂z=(t−s)2=t2−2st+s2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get ∂x∂t=3,∂y∂t=1,∂z∂t=2s.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂t=(−sin⁡3t)⋅3+(4st2−4s2t)⋅1+(t2−2st+s2)⋅2s=−3sin⁡3t+4st2−4s2t+2st2−4s2t+2s3=−3sin⁡3t+6st2−8s2t+2s3.

Finally, c1=6, c2=−8 and c3=2, and therefore c1+c2+c3=6+(−8)+2=0.

q-94589.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14155924/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-6z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)+2(s+3t)=2st+2s+6t \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2st \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-6(2s-t)=6t-12s\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =3 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(2st+2s+6t)\cdot s+(2st)\cdot 3+(6t-12s)\cdot (-1) \\  & =2{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{2}+6st+6st-6t+12s \\  & =2{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{2}+12st+12s-6t \\  & =2({s}^{2}t+{s}^{2}+6st+6s-3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}={c}_{2}=6,{c}_{3}=-3,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=6+6-3=9.
$$

Question 18
?

Let f(x,y,z)=x2+2xy−3z2, where x=st, y=s+3t, and z=2s−t. Given that ∂f∂t=2(s2t+s2+c1st+c2s+c3t),

find the value of c1+c2+c3.

a
−3
b
−6
c
3
d
9
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows:

∂f∂t=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂t+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂t+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂t.

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z:

∂f∂x=2x+2y,∂f∂y=2x,∂f∂z=−6z.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get

∂f∂x=2(st)+2(s+3t)=2st+2s+6t∂f∂y=2st∂f∂z=−6(2s−t)=6t−12s

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to t, and we get

∂x∂t=s∂y∂t=3∂z∂t=−1.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

∂f∂t=(2st+2s+6t)⋅s+(2st)⋅3+(6t−12s)⋅(−1)=2s2t+2s2+6st+6st−6t+12s=2s2t+2s2+12st+12s−6t=2(s2t+s2+6st+6s−3t)

Finally, c1=c2=6,c3=−3, and therefore c1+c2+c3=6+6−3=9.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$

Let f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+z2, where x=s2+t2, y=st and z=st2. Given that ∂f∂s=3s2t+c1t+c2st+c3st4, find the value of c1+c2+c3.

a
−6
b
5
c
4
d
3
e
−1

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=y,∂f∂y=x+z,∂f∂z=y+2z.

Writing the above results in terms of s and t, we get ∂f∂x=st,∂f∂y=s2+t2+st2,∂f∂z=st+2st2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=2s,∂y∂s=1t,∂z∂s=t2.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=(st)⋅2s+(s2+t2+st2)⋅1t+(st+2st2)⋅t2=2s2t+s2t+t+st+st+2st4=3s2t+t+2st+2st4.

Finally, c1=1, c2=2 and c3=2, and therefore c1+c2+c3=1+2+2=5.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(-1)\cdot {e}^{s}+(-1)\cdot 1+(1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-{e}^{s}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Let f(x,y,z)=z−x−y, where x=es+t, y=s+1 and z=1−t−s. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
es
b
−es−2
c
es−2t
d
−es+t
e
es+2+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y,z) with two independent variables s and t, where x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t) and z=z(s,t), can be expressed as follows: ∂f∂s=∂f∂x⋅∂x∂s+∂f∂y⋅∂y∂s+∂f∂z⋅∂z∂s

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x,y and z: ∂f∂x=−1,∂f∂y=−1,∂f∂z=1.

Next, we take the derivatives of x, y, and z with respect to s, and we get ∂x∂s=es,∂y∂s=1,∂z∂s=−1.

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get ∂f∂s=(−1)⋅es+(−1)⋅1+(1)⋅(−1)=−es−2.
